Stress is indicated by the stress mark [ˈ] before the stressed syllable, and is marked only when it is not predictable. Unless indicated otherwise, verbs and deverbatives are always stressed on the root. Nouns and other parts of speech are stressed on the first syllable. Affixes, whether flexional or derivational, are never stressed. ... sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title: van Driem 1988 (Pacific Linguistics C-104 festschrift chapter on the *-t directive suffix). The 'prosodic' hit is from the volume title, but the chapter is open access (DOI 10.15144/PL-C104.157 -> sealang PDF, saved to and footnote 8 on p. 167 gives a full first-hand Baksila Dumi stress statement: weak, non-distinctive; verbs/deverbatives on the stem, nouns and other classes on the first syllable, affixes never stressed, reflexive infinitives on -si. This is the same rule as the catalog's van Driem 1993 p. 58 quote (now available in open text instead of snippets) and is corroborated by the on-disk van Driem 1988 LTBA paper (p. 174: inflected-verb stress 'regular, i.e. on the verb root'). Nothing new bears on the Rai 2016 (Makpa) penultimate rule, so the catalog's 'conflict' classification is unchanged; the new source refines the van Driem side (reflexive -si exception) and does not supersede the 1993 grammar as deciding source. the download was done via DOI resolution and Crossref.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Dumi is weak and nondistinctive. I indicate stress in Dumi forms by the stress mark ['] preceding the stressed syllable only when it is not predictable. Unless otherwise indicated: affixes, whether inflectional or derivational, do not carry the stress. Verbs and deverbatives take the stress on the stem. Nouns and other parts of speech are stressed on the first syllable. Infinitives of reflexive verbs invariably take the stress on the reflexive suffix si, but I have chosen to mark the stress in these infinitives. Inflected forms of reflexive verbs carry the stress on the stem.

new_statements.reading: Same author, same dialect (Baksila) and essentially the same wording as the catalog's van Driem 1993 p. 58 deciding quote, but here read in full open text rather than Google Books snippets. Stress is weak and non-contrastive; placement is morphological: verb stem for verbs and deverbatives, first syllable for nouns and other parts of speech, affixes never stressed, with one stated exception class (reflexive infinitives stressed on -si). It does not touch the Makpa-dialect penultimate rule of Rai 2016, so the catalog's 'conflict' coding stands; it upgrades the strength of the evidence of the van Driem side from snippet to open text and adds the reflexive-infinitive exception.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were re-opened and confirmed at their stated locators: van Driem 1993 p. 58 via five overlapping Google Books snippets held by the project, Rai 2016 sec. 4.5.2 p. 103 (plus ch. 4 summary and ch. 15 e) in the full dissertation text. The classification ('conflict': van Driem = morphologically placed weak stress, verbs on root / nouns initial / affixes unstressed; Rai = non-distinctive, penultimate across word classes, with trisyllabic nouns sam'baki, bi'rʌsi contradicting noun-initial) rests on the two reference grammars that Glottolog 5.1 lists as the only grammars of the language; The open van Driem 1988 LTBA article was downloaded and scanned; its only stress statement (p. 173, verb stress regular on the root, reflexive infinitive -si stressed

sources.note: The paper is about the morphology of a directive suffix (the 'prosodic' keyword comes from the festschrift title), but footnote 8 gives a complete first-hand statement of Dumi (Baksila) word-stress placement: weak, non-distinctive; verbs/deverbatives stressed on the stem, nouns and other word classes on the first syllable, affixes never stressed, unpredictable cases marked lexically; reflexive infinitives stressed on the suffix -si, inflected reflexives on the stem.
